query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The excellent corrosion resistance of steels in chemical‐processing and nuclear‐power applications is primarily due to the formation of a dense, chromium‐enriched passive oxide film. This film is promoted by a refined microstructure that accelerates Cr diffusion (especially along high-angle grain boundaries), thereby rapidly renewing the protective film under aggressive conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional stainless or duplex steels with a coarse-grained microstructure and standard Cr content.
generation.intervention: Apply severe plastic deformation (e.g., high-pressure torsion) or similar grain-refining processing to create a fine-grained, high grain-boundary density microstructure while maintaining or slightly increasing Cr content.
generation.conditions: Exposure to corrosive environments typical of chemical-processing (e.g., saline solutions) and nuclear-power settings (e.g., high-temperature water or molten salt environments) at operating temperatures and pressures.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, chromium-enriched passive oxide layer (likely Cr2O3) preferentially formed at and along refined grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The enhanced grain-boundary density accelerates Cr migration from the bulk to the surface, facilitating quick formation and repair of a protective Cr-oxide layer. This uniform passivation limits ion dissolution, reduces local galvanic effects, and prevents pitting, even under high-temperature or aggressive chemical exposures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to coarse-grained steels, grain-refined steels will exhibit a lower corrosion current density, a more positive (noble) corrosion potential, and fewer or smaller pits under identical corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained steels processed by conventional routes without deliberate microstructural refinement.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply under conditions where corrosion is governed by chemical attack (as in aqueous chloride systems or high-temperature water) and where the integrity of the passive film can form undisturbed. It may not extend to environments dominated by mechanical wear or where the passive film is continuously disrupted.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of grain-boundary assisted Cr diffusion versus possible galvanic effects in dual-phase steels remain to be quantitatively defined. Variations in other alloying elements may also influence the protective film’s stability in complex environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of steel samples: one with a conventional coarse-grained microstructure and another subjected to severe plastic deformation to obtain a refined grain structure. Expose both groups to a controlled corrosive environment (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl solution at elevated temperature and, separately, a simulated high-temperature water environment representative of nuclear reactor conditions). Use advanced surface analysis (e.g., XPS, SKP) to quantify the Cr content and continuity of the passive film. Perform potentiodynamic polarization tests to determine corrosion potentials and current densities.
measurements: Cr concentration and uniformity in the passive film (via XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the refined-grain steels do not exhibit significantly enhanced Cr enrichment in the passive film and demonstrate lower corrosion rates (i.e., lower Icorr and a more noble Ecorr) compared to the coarse-grained samples under the same test conditions, then the hypothesis stating that grain refinement enhances corrosion resistance via accelerated Cr passivation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Development of materials suitable for molten fluoride salt environments started in the 1950s with the Aircraft Reactor Experiment (ARE). This experiment used Inconel 600 as a container material, however it was found that this material was not be suitable for high temperature molten fluoride salt applications. The Molten Salt Reactor Experiment (MSRE) at ORNL led to the development of Hastelloy N alloy as a structural material for fuel-bearing molten fluoride salt, which was demonstrated to have superior long-term corrosion resistance in molten fluoride salts. However, in fuel bearing molten salts, the fission product tellurium was noted to lead to crack formation in the alloy due to the precipitation of intermetallic compounds at the grain boundaries. In addition, in such high Ni-content alloys, additional embrittlement may be caused during irradiation. Transmutation of Ni can lead to the formation of helium that weaken the alloy grain boundaries. Several other traditional high temperature alloys have been tested in molten fluoride salts such as 316 L and 304 stainless steels, Incoloy 800 H, Inconel 617, Inconel 625, Hastelloy X, and Haynes 230.

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed.
